On 10/30/12 5:08 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Tuesday, October 30, 2012 4:17:35 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
>     On Tuesday, October 30, 2012 3:16:46 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
>
>         The model is generally a memory hog (what with so many covariance matrices) and consumes most of the available
>         16GB of RAM on my machine during the run.  I know I may improve the speed from the attached script by directly
>         augmenting lp__ in a fashion that composes the quadratic product without performing inverses of covariance
>         matrices.   Since I still need the cholesky decomposition and the inverse of that, I'm not clear that this
>         approach would conserve RAM.
>
>
>     In R, you can pass a pars argument to stan() that names the posterior quantities you would like to keep. Using that
>     would give R more headroom to calculate afterward.
>
>     But the main place where I think RAM is consumed unnecessarily is with the covariance matrices in the transformed
>     parameters block:

These are two different kinds of memory requirements.

The transformed params (and anything else involved in the
model) is a transient memory demand.  As soon as you get
the gradient, the memory's recovered.

The parameters that are saved in memory (in RStan, not
in Stan itself, which streams the samples to file) are
a constant, growing memory demand.

I actually don't think covar matrix transforms cause too
much of a hit, but it could be improved.

Anything that involves solving is going to be way worse,
because we build up the full expression tree.

The best thing we can do throughout Stan to improve
efficiency is to partially evaluate auto-dif.   We could
do more of this in all of our matrix ops.  Right now,
there are some efficient products and dot products, and
a few functions like sum(), and quite few auto-dif efficient
vectorized distributions.

- Bob

On 10/30/12 3:16 PM, terrance savitsky wrote:
> The attached monster model ran under stan - much faster than i'd thought, though I wasn't able to check for convergence
> because I received the following error in (64-bit) R: Error: cannot allocate vector of size 16 Kb.

Sounds like R's out of memory.

By dumping your data, you can run Stan from
the command line, which will stream out samples
rather than trying to keep them in memory.

I'd be curious as to hwo much of the memory is R
and how much is Stan's model execution.

You can try more thinning within R.

The profile should be gradually increasing memory
due to saving samples, plus spikes as the model
is evaluated every leapfrog step.

That should use as much memory the first time
being executed as any other time, so you can
probably watch whatever OS your using's system
monitor to watch memory.

 >  There are some
> things I may try in R, but I write to see if anyone has experience managing memory allocations to arrays in R.   The
> model is generally a memory hog (what with so many covariance matrices) and consumes most of the available 16GB of RAM
> on my machine during the run.  I know I may improve the speed from the attached script by directly augmenting lp__ in a
> fashion that composes the quadratic product without performing inverses of covariance matrices.   Since I still need the
> cholesky decomposition and the inverse of that, I'm not clear that this approach would conserve RAM.   Also, even if I
> could conserve RAM, I bet I'd still hit the vector allocation size limit.
>
> I also received a few warning statements (during 2000 iterations) that said this:
>
> Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal
> (really) issue (and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Error in function
> stan::prob::ordered_logistic(N4stan5agrad3varE): Cut points parameter is 1.#INF:0, but must be finite!
> If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
>   If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be drawn from the psoterior.

I was hoping that message would be less scary than
"(Non-fatal Warning)" followed by "Error in function..."

I'll fix the spelling of "posterior".

Any other suggestions for how to say this given that the "Error in function..
must be finite!" part is fixed.

> Cutpoints are generally notorious highly intracorrelated under ordered logistic models, but I do something that I want
> to check if you think it is a problem.   I fix the first element of a vector of ordered cutpoints to 0 to achieve hard
> identifiability.   the other elements are random.

It's not so much an identifiability problem as a problem
with the discretization in the Hamiltonian simulation.

For example, if you have a small value for a scale parameter
sigma bounded below at zero, and a gradient toward zero and
a large step size, it's possible to overshoot zero in one
leapfrog step inside the Hamiltonian simulation.  Lower step
sizes can always be found (up to arithmetic issues), but we
can't get around the fact that we're using a first order
(derivative only) discretization of the Hamiltonian.

- Bob

something that would be useful is a user option to pre-select the parameters that will be returned / written to file.   such a feature may be useful for managing memory for running stan within R.

messages.body_plain:
Are you running in R or from the command line?

Do you know if everything fits in memory without
swapping?

Do you have anything like a reasonable way to
initialize?  It can make a big difference in
a model like this.  You might also try the zero
init option because that'll make all the unbounded
coefficients zero, which is usually an easier place
to start than drawing a value for beta[1] and then

Did you run fewer than 40K iterations to see
if you're converging?  The default is to use the
entire first half of each chain for adaptation,
so you can speed up nearly a factor of 2 if you
are converging earlier.

Also, I'd recommend running for shorter periods
first just to see how things are going.

What would also really help here is a

    poisson_log(y|alpha) = poisson(y|exp(alpha))

> model {
>      // implicit: sig ~ uniform(.01,1.4142);

This will be initialized between (.14,1.3), so low values could be
problematic given the hierarchical model.  It looks like you
really wanted variances on (0.0001,2) -- that's what you get
in terms of range, but it's not quite uniform because of the square
transform (you need to add the Jacobian adjustment if you want it
to be uniform on variances).

>      // implicit: intercept ~ uniform(-40,20);

Initial values will be in the range (-34,14).

In general, Stan's default is to use uniform inits between [-2,2]
on the unconstrained params.  For bounded params, that amounts
to a range of

   (inv_logit(-2), inv_logit(2)) = (.12,.88)

So you sample from the central 80% interval, but non-uniformly on
the transformed space because of the logit transform.  I should write
this into the manual as an example along with positive-only inits,
which are also common.

>      beta[1] ~ normal(0,100);

Initialized on range (-2,2) uniformly.

>      district_season_eff ~ normal(0, 1);
>      for(q in 2:(Q + 1))
>          beta[q] ~ normal(beta[q-1],sig);

Here you can apply the Matt trick, which would look
as follows, and should significantly speed up sampling
speed (despite adding some extra named variables -- if you
don't want to write out the beta[] values, you can define
them instead as local variables in the model instead of as
transformed params).

parameters {
     vector[J] beta[Q+1] beta_raw;
}
transformed parameters {
     vector[J] beta[Q+1] beta;

     beta[1] <- beta_raw[1] / 100;
     for (q in 2:(Q + 1))
       beta[q] = (beta_raw[q] + beta[q-1]) / sigma;
}
model {
     beta_raw ~ normal(0,1);
}

I haven't compiled it, but I'm pretty sure all the vector
ops here are kosher.

This also conveniently vectorizes the normal draw
for the entire vectored time series including the initial point.

- Bob

> On 11/2/12 2:59 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > This is unnecessarily slow, and I believe it will also yield the wrong answer in Stan because you have specified a bunch
> > of conditional distributions for the betas whose product is not equal to the joint distribution of the betas.
>
> Why not?  Isn't this the usual way to do a time series?
> Isn't the joint just as follows:
>
>     p(beta[1]) * PROD_{q in 2:(Q+1)} p(beta[q]|beta[q-1])

You're right. The joint distribution is improper because of the unit-root, so I was having trouble wrapping my head around it being the product of proper distributions. Usually for a random walk, there would be an improper prior on beta[1]. It is fine to put a prior with finite variance on beta[1]; it just is somewhat odd to have it have a difference variance than the rest of the series.

Anyway, we're in agreement that the fastest way is to parameterize the noise and along the lines of what Bob said

beta[q] <- beta[q - 1] + sig * beta_noise[q];

with iid standard normal priors on beta_noise is best.

Ben

On Friday, November 2, 2012 7:27:06 PM UTC-4, Ted wrote:
> The code posted below compiled and is running with one chain at 1000 iterations now.  However, I don't understand the lp__ stuff conceptually so I'm not sure if the code that I adapted from Ben's reply is correct.  Would you mind checking it out for me?

Attached is how I would do it with a few simplifying tweaks. There is stuff on the

lp__ <- lp__ + whatever;

syntax in the manual and also an entry in the FAQ

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/4dwmJj1YwbsJ

It is primarily intended for distributions that Stan doesn't have yet and manual Jacobian determinants and odd things like that. But sometimes it is just faster to use that syntax than to use the log density that Stan has, such as the Poisson which isn't currently vectorized and entails an unnecessary logarithm.

Since the Poisson density is

f(y | lambda) = lambda^y * exp(-lambda) / y!

its log is

log(f(y | lambda)) = y * log(lambda) - lambda - log(y!)

and the log(y!) is a constant so you don't need to account for it. All you need to do is sum that over the observations and add it to log priors to get the log-posterior (lp__).

Ben

On this webpage http://mc-stan.org/windows-install.html, in which the steps of installing Rtools are presented. Make sure you have done

Select Additional Tasks: check Edit Path and Save Version in Registry, click Next,

messages.subject: Model advice sought for EEG time-series data
messages.subject_clean: Model advice sought for EEG time-series data
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

I work in cognitive science where it is common to record electroencephalographic (eeg) voltage data while presenting various stimuli to participants. A typical analysis strategy for such data is to cut up the time-series data from each participant into pieces according to when the stimuli were presented, grabbing, say, two seconds (200 time samples) of eeg data from each stimulus onset time. The by-time-sample average of these pieces is then computed for each participant and stimulus type, and finally the by-time-sample average and CI is computed across participants for each stimulus, which are then compared to one another. (R code demonstrating this typical procedure is here: https://gist.github.com/4040541)

It strikes me that a better approach might be to explicitly model the influence of the different stimuli on the continuous eeg time-series data, where the time-series is assumed to be otherwise noisy and autoregressive. However, I'm not sure how to properly operationalize the stimulus influence function in a manner that is flexible enough to capture the various stimulus effect waveforms we tend to see (while all waveforms eventually decay in effect over time, some have an initial positive effect while others have an initial negative effect, and some have complicated waveforms with multiple bumps across time before decaying back to baseline).

Any advice?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology
Dalhousie University

Looking to arrange a meeting? Check my public calendar: http://goo.gl/BYH99

~ Certainty is folly... I think. ~

messages.subject: Convergence issues in a non-GLM Bernoulli-logit model
messages.subject_clean: Convergence issues in a non-GLM Bernoulli-logit model
messages.body_plain:
So, Stan is awesome. It's fast enough that it's making my current study, which entails fitting models of intertemporal choice to human subjects in real time, possible. Hooray!

Currently, I'm having trouble getting my chains to converge consistently. This goes for several models, but let's at least begin by considering a model that in general works fine but for a particular dataset has trouble converging in one of the parameters. Load the attached R source (the Stan code is a string literal) and try something like:

m = stan_model(model_code = code)
fit = sampling(m, data = dat, chains = 7)
summary(fit)$summary[c("v30", "scurve", "rho"), "Rhat"]

As a rule, the Rhat for rho will be above 1.1, typically at 1.5 or 2.0. Tweaking iter, warmup, thin, or init doesn't seem to help.

I can get convergence if I restrict the support of rho to [0, .11] or [.1, 1] (and set iter to something big), but not, e.g., [.01, .99]. Looking at plots, I would guess that the lumpiness of rho's marginal density is to blame. But I don't know what to do about it.

(The reason why the supports of v30 and scurve aren't [0, 1], if you're wondering, is to avoid floating-point overflows leading to NaNs. Formerly, I had a fancier way around this where I switched to a logarithmic approximation (heavily abusing Stan's step() to compensate for the lack of conditional expressions with real numbers), but then I began getting error message about Stan not being able to find a small enough step size.)

Hi, I ran my model, again, after some help from Ben and Bob such that less memory is drawn by the autodiff and I employed the 'pars' option to restrict returned parameters.   I still ran out of memory (using R) as stan attempted to write out objects to file.  I'm able to store a lot more parameters for the same number of stored iterations in JAGS without a problem.  Since I assume both JAGS and stan store the sampled parameters in similar (S4) objects, I'm wondering if the storing the last state of the sampler requires also storing the last gradient computation and if this may be an issue.  Also, this time when the sampler finished, I had a message indicating the iterations were completed as well as the out of memory message.  Yet, the object existed and when I attempted to extract samples, it told me that there were no samples.   I did not receive any indication that the sampler encountered issues, however.

On Thu, Nov 1, 2012 at 11:11 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
>
> On 10/30/12 5:08 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > On Tuesday, October 30, 2012 4:17:35 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> >
> >     On Tuesday, October 30, 2012 3:16:46 PM UTC-4, tds151 wrote:
> >
> >         The model is generally a memory hog (what with so many covariance matrices) and consumes most of the available
> >         16GB of RAM on my machine during the run.  I know I may improve the speed from the attached script by directly
> >         augmenting lp__ in a fashion that composes the quadratic product without performing inverses of covariance
> >         matrices.   Since I still need the cholesky decomposition and the inverse of that, I'm not clear that this
> >         approach would conserve RAM.
> >
> >
> >     In R, you can pass a pars argument to stan() that names the posterior quantities you would like to keep. Using that
> >     would give R more headroom to calculate afterward.
> >
> >     But the main place where I think RAM is consumed unnecessarily is with the covariance matrices in the transformed
> >     parameters block:
>
> These are two different kinds of memory requirements.
>
> The transformed params (and anything else involved in the
> model) is a transient memory demand.  As soon as you get
> the gradient, the memory's recovered.
>
> The parameters that are saved in memory (in RStan, not
> in Stan itself, which streams the samples to file) are
> a constant, growing memory demand.
>
> I actually don't think covar matrix transforms cause too
> much of a hit, but it could be improved.
>
> Anything that involves solving is going to be way worse,
> because we build up the full expression tree.
>
> The best thing we can do throughout Stan to improve
> efficiency is to partially evaluate auto-dif.   We could
> do more of this in all of our matrix ops.  Right now,
> there are some efficient products and dot products, and
> a few functions like sum(), and quite few auto-dif efficient
> vectorized distributions.

>
>
> - Bob
>
> --
>
>

Thanks for the report.

You can always write the models to file rather than
storing them in R using the command-line version of Stan.
That just streams the draws to a file, so there's no overhead
at all for number of samples.

back into a Stan object.

I don't know how we're storing data in R (but I'm guessing
we're about to find out).  The original plan was
to store the data in a compact C++ object and access it
through Rcpp, but that proved to be a huge hassle for saving
and restoring across sessions.  I still have some hope we
could write custom serialization but I'm not really enough of
an R programmer to do it myself and it didn't sound easy after
a query to the Rcpp list.

Because users really wanted to be able to save sessions,
we switched the code to store the data in R rather than in
C (hopefully it's not being duplicated -- if so, we could
probably cut out a lot of fat there).

- Bob

messages.subject: memory in R and RStan
messages.subject_clean: memory in R and RStan
messages.body_plain:
On 11/12/12 5:37 PM, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> [to stan-dev]
>
> 1. reading csv files of samples in RStan
>
> Currently, no functionality in RStan to do that.  I guess I should work on it so maybe in the release after 1.0.4, we
> can have it.

This would be really useful for scalability in R or even
just for running from Stan command line and then
reading into R for later analysis.

> 2. keeping `samples so far'
>
> I do not know now.  I have never encounter an error in R of `out of memory`.

Lucky you.

If you use 32-bit R and try to run JAGS models,
you'll run into it fast enough.   I rewrote some models in
Stan that took up way less memory than their JAGS counterparts
in R.

Any model that calls iterative solvers on matrices may
take up a lot of memory during sampling the way things are
implemented now.  The issue is that we build up the entire
expression tree over the iterations before propagating the
chain rule backwards for calculating gradients.  We plan to
make this more efficient by extracting the double values,
calling the iterative algorithsm on those, then partially
evaluating the gradients using all the rules in The Matrix
Cookbook and Magnus and Neudecker's book.

> I do not know how R or OS deals with this
> case.  And in the case if it is R calling a C++ function that is running out of memory, I am not sure we can do
> something in R then.

It's going to be handled by process.  When R calls the
C function, it's all in the same process, and so sharing
all the memory from the OSes point of view.  Thus if you run
R in 32-bit mode, the OS is going to put a low ceiling on
how much memory can be used.  A C function called from R
might not be well behaved with respect to R -- it can call its
own malloc() and play havoc with R's memory model.

I don't know how well Rcpp deals with these issues and how
much is up to the user.

You can try something like object.size() in R.  memory.profile()
also looks useful.

There may also be extra objects hanging around in the R environment
taking up space that have nothing to do with Stan.  R uses
garbage collection, but doesn't appear to do it very well.  So
one probably shouldn't use long-running R sessions even if you get
rid of local variables and call gc() to try to clean things up.

 > In short, it is difficult.  Unless this happens a lot, I would not put the investigation on top
> priority.

We should probably test the scalability to make sure we're
not doing something sub-optimally.  If it's a deep issue with
R, I agree that it's not a priority for us to try to fix it!

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
It is confusing because

   C++/Java:  0-indexed, row-major
   R/BUGS:    1-indexed, column-major

Our data types are all described very thoroughly
in the manual.  Matrices are matrices, vectors
are column vectors unless declared as row_vector.
If you have a matrix a, then a[2] is a row vector (which
I'm told is very confusing whether you're used to MATLAB
or R -- it seemed natural enough to me coming from
a more functional programming perspective).

We also reduce result types.  So that if x is
a row vector and y is a column vector, then
x*y is a real type, not a 1 x 1 vector.  And unlike
R, these types don't auto-coerce everywhere.

And we promote argument types.  So that if you add
a scalar and a vector, the scalar is treated like
a vector with the scalar in each position.

In the multi_normal distribution, we allow either
a row vector or column vector for the mean (I was
overruled on type checking there because the other
developers liked the flexibility and argued it'd
be less confusing to users to not have to always
make the vector a column vector).

- Bob

messages.subject: Array literals?
messages.subject_clean: Array literals?
messages.body_plain:
I've been working on an R package to generate Stan code from typical glmer formulas. It's working fine so far. One issue I've had to work around is the absence of array literals, which would be handy in multi_normal statements where varying effects are routinely zero-centered.

I tried the expected C syntax of {0,0,0} for example, which of course doesn't work.

Any plans to add array literals? It's not a necessary addition, as I've used transformed data to generate the needed vector of zeros. But if it's easy to get the parser to recognize the C syntax, that would make the code easier to read, which would fulfill some of my teaching and consulting objectives.

Stan is continuing to be fantastic, by the way. About to submit my first paper based on Stan simulations.

> which would fulfill some of my teaching and consulting objectives.

Things have stabilized after the release somewhat,
so we were just discussing the to-do list in today's
meeting.

We're still going to prioritize bug fixes, arithmetic
stability issues, and error trapping/reporting, but
we're also deciding what to do next.

C/C++/Java don't truly have array literals because
you can only use them in declarations.  I can't do
something like:

    sort({1,7,3})

with "{1,7,3}" being a literal.

We are going to add true array/vector/row-vector literals.
We haven't finalized the syntax yet, but I like the very
explicit forms:

    array(x1,...,xN)
    vector(x1,...,XN)
    row_vector(x1,...,XN)

This is along the lines of R's multi-purpose c(x1,...,xN).

I also like the use of grouped variables with "(...)" in Python.
It lets you do things like:

   (x,y) = foo(a,b,c);

where foo returns a pair, the first element of which is
assigned to x and the second to y.

There are all sorts of other array processing issues
we'll eventually add, like slicing such as x[1:3,2:5,7]
producing a 3 x 4 array result.

> Stan is continuing to be fantastic, by the way. About to submit my first paper based on Stan simulations.

Thanks, and thanks for the feedback.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Convergence issues in a non-GLM Bernoulli-logit model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Convergence issues in a non-GLM Bernoulli-logit model
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, November 12, 2012 3:14:43 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> You might want to try simplifying the parameterization.
> For a start, why not characterize parameter a directy instead of
> in terms of scurve, curve and e?

My motivation behind the hairy parametrization is basically to keep the parameters interpretable. As the model is now, v30 is the discounted value of a reward at 30 days (so if v30 = .6, the subject would be indifferent between receiving $100 today and receiving $60 in 30 days), scurve controls how flat the discounting curve is (such that scurve = 0 makes an exponential curve, scurve = 1 makes a curve that is almost everywhere a horizontal line, and the transition between the two bounds "feels" linear given graphs on human scales), and rho controls how sensitive the subject is to differences between options (such that when rho = 0, the subject chooses completely at random, and when rho = 1, the subject is practically deterministic). Of course, I could compute marginal densities of such quantities regardless of the parameterization. The problem with parameters that are hard to interpret, as I see it, is that the priors are then really hard to interpret. And even though I don't want genuinely informative priors in this case, since I'm comparing models and the setting is the lab instead of the real world, I still have to worry about issues like the scale of the priors. For example, under one, more natural parameterization for this model, curvature of the discounting function varies such that a range of curvatures with large differences for behavior have the same prior mass as a range of curvatures with small differences for behavior. In effect, the latter range would be favored, although this is undesirable. Is there a nicer way around this sort of problem than using interpretable parameters?

As for putting rho in [0, 1] instead of [0, 10], that's just because 1 is a rounder number than 10.

> It can also help to regularize the data.

 Rescaling the time values (ssd and lld) would change the meaning of v30, but rescaling the reward values (ssr and ssd) has, to my surprise, solved the problem, at least in this case. The chains converge fine now. Thanks! I'll see how far rescaling can take me. (And now that I think about it, perhaps I could keep the meaning of v30 for rescaled time values if I altered the calculation of a appropriately.)

> You could move any of the transformed parameters you don't
> care about reporting to be local variables in the model.

 Good point, I'm not sure why I didn't do that to begin with.

messages.body_plain:
That gets a little tricky.

1) You will need to update all 4 definitions of the distribution function. I'm assuming you've done that successfully. If not, the policy type will match the fourth argument and the behavior won't be as expected.
2) You need to update stanc. The place you'll need to touch is src/stan/gm/function_signatures.hpp. You'll need to update the function signature accepted by the parser for ordered_logistic_log.

Once all that's done, you should be able to get away with it.

If you're just altering generated code, you won't need to do step 2.

messages.body_plain:
I'm still not sure I understand the intention, so please
bear with my trying to rephrase it with more concrete types:

   int<lower=0> N;                   // number of data items
   int<lower=2> K;                   // max number of cats
   int<lower=1,upper=K> y[N];        // outcome
   int<lower=2,upper=K> ncats[N];    // number of possible cats

The constraint on y is tighter than can be declared in Stan,

   y[n] in 1:ncats[n].

and here's the part we don't yet support:

   ragged_matrix[K-1] c;          // cutpoint vecs in rows

For instance, with K=5, we might have

   c = [c1 ;
        c2 c3 ;
        c4 c5 c6 ;
        c7 c8 c9 c10]

so that c[1] is a 1-row-vector [c1],
c[2] is the 2-row-vector [c2 c3], and so on.

And then what you want to do model-wise is something like this:

   for (n in 1:N) {
     eta[n] <- ...;  // calculate predictor
     y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(eta[n], c[ncuts[n]]');
   }

Before getting into how Stan can deal with this, can you let
us know if this is your intent?

- Bob

Looking at it, I figured it was something like this.

The alternative is to keep the data/parameters on a regularized
scale and then compute generated_quantities that are interpretable
by scaling.  This helps rather than hurts for specifying "default"
priors.  (In general, whatever priors you use, you should check sensitivity
to prior assumptions.)

> As the model is now,
> v30 is the discounted value of a reward at 30 days (so if v30 = .6, the subject would be indifferent between receiving
> $100 today and receiving $60 in 30 days), scurve controls how flat the discounting curve is (such that scurve = 0 makes
> an exponential curve, scurve = 1 makes a curve that is almost everywhere a horizontal line, and the transition between
> the two bounds "feels" linear given graphs on human scales), and rho controls how sensitive the subject is to
> differences between options (such that when rho = 0, the subject chooses completely at random, and when rho = 1, the
> subject is practically deterministic). Of course, I could compute marginal densities of such quantities regardless of
> the parameterization. The problem with parameters that are hard to interpret, as I see it, is that the priors are then
> really hard to interpret. And even though I don't want genuinely informative priors in this case, since I'm comparing
> models and the setting is the lab instead of the real world, I still have to worry about issues like the scale of the
> priors. For example, under one, more natural parameterization for this model, curvature of the discounting function
> varies such that a range of curvatures with large differences for behavior have the same prior mass as a range of
> curvatures with small differences for behavior. In effect, the latter range would be favored, although this is
> undesirable. Is there a nicer way around this sort of problem than using interpretable parameters?
>
> As for putting rho in [0, 1] instead of [0, 10], that's just because 1 is a rounder number than 10.

:-)

>     It can also help to regularize the data.
>
>
>   Rescaling the time values (ssd and lld) would change the meaning of v30, but rescaling the reward values (ssr and ssd)
> has, to my surprise, solved the problem, at least in this case. The chains converge fine now. Thanks! I'll see how far
> rescaling can take me. (And now that I think about it, perhaps I could keep the meaning of v30 for rescaled time values
> if I altered the calculation of a appropriately.)

One reason this can happen is that all the chains might be more
likely to start in the region of the same mode.  If that happens,
it can appear like convergence when you're not really exploring
the entire posterior.  In some cases, this can be OK if you know
there's only one reasonable mode and know where to look for it,
or if there are several equivalent modes in a non-identifiable model.

Did you ever check the traceplots to see what was going on in cases
that didn't converge?

- Bob

messages.subject: tips on improving mixing in a multivariate mixed response model
messages.subject_clean: tips on improving mixing in a multivariate mixed response model
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I've posted a model on this board a few times, along the way, that inputs multiple responses, each as multivariate matrices.   They are all linked through the sharing of sets of multivariate random effects.   Ben worked with me to optimize the auto diff processing and RAM management.   Let's focus on one of the sets of multivariate random effects, Delta[t,d].   Running stan for 2500 iterations (of which 1000 are burnin) demonstrates terribly poor mixing of Delta (as shown in the attached plots. Each plot contains a random selection of Delta[t,d] parameters).   Essentially both of the chains I instantiate barely move.   I run a similar model in JAGS, but under conjugate priors - e.g. Wishart priors on the precision matrices of the sets of multivariate random effects, such as Delta).   I wanted to employ a less informative construction, and so imposed uniform priors on the correlation matrices under stan.   Anyway, the mixing in JAGS is very good.

stan is forced to choose very small step sizes to make the chain go.   This performance counters my intuition for the random walk suppression of NUTS.   The only idea that occurs to me is that 3 of the 6 response matrices are ordinal.   Some of the associated cutpoints (that lack observations) mix poorly in JAGS, though such does not affect the robust mixing of the random effects, Delta, there.  Since NUTS moves the entire parameter space on each iteration, I wonder if all the step sizes for all the parameters may be constrained by a poorly mixing subset.   Such would not seem to be the case (unless there is a high correlation among them that is not ameliorated by the hamiltonian).

Thanks for any tips you would offer.

--
Thank you, Terrance Savitsky

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: employing a ragged array of cutpoints
messages.body_plain:
It is too bad there's not an elegant way to do this
within Stan.  We could handle this case with a triangular
matrix data type -- we wouldn't even need full ragged arrays.
We'll probably add one in the near future (months, not weeks
or days, that is).

As to some of the other proposed solutions, you don't want
unnecessary "junk" parameters as they'll distort the
posterior geometry and what the U-turn condition in
NUTS does (there are ways to mitigate their effect,
but it's still work by the algorithm).

Here's one solution that stays entirely within
Stan's modeling language and doesn't add any
unnecessary parameters.   But it does make you recode things
like ordered vectors from scratch in the model.

Suppose you have K maximum possible outcome categories, which
means anywhere from 1 to (K-1) cut points per instance.
Suppose K=5, then I'm proposing a representation like this:

outcomes  num_cuts  lowest      increments
2         1         first[1]
3         2         first[2]    inc[1]
4         3         first[3]    inc[2] inc[3]
5         4         first[4]    inc[4] inc[5] inc[6]

Then the 3 cutpoints for the case of 4 outcomes
are (lowest[3], lowest[3]+inc[2], lowest[3]+inc[2]+inc[3]).
The rest is just a bunch of by-hand triangular array
indexing, which is majorly ugly.

There's some indexing arithmetic below to compute the
starting indexes 1, 2, and 4 for he increments.
Note that each is the sum of the number of entries in
the previous row, so takes the form of the sum of integers
from 1 to some number (plus 1 because we went with
R-style matrix indexing).

Anyway, here goes.

parameters {
   real first_cuts[K-1];
   real<lower=0> incr_cuts[((K-1)*(K-2))/ 2];
}
model {

   // priors on cutpoints
   first_cuts ~  ...;
   incr_cuts ~ ...;

   for (n in 1:N) {

     // build up cutpoint vector
     vector[num_cuts[n]] c;
     c[1] <- first_cuts[num_cuts[n]];
     for (k in 2:num_cuts[n])
       c[k] <- c[k-1]
               + incr_cuts[((num_cuts[n]-1)*(num_cuts[n]-2))/2 + k - 1];

     // linear predictor (local var or transformed eta[n] if saving)
     eta <- ...;

     // likelihood
     y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(eta,c);

   }

I haven't compiled this, so no guarantees on perfect
well-formedness.

The amount of work done to create new vectors (it requires
a malloc then free under the hood by our matrix lib) and all the
arithmetic and copying will probably be dwarfed by the
other operations, which include inverse logits (hence exponentials)
and their derivatives.   (The allocations could be reduced
by sorting the data based on number of cut points and then
indexing into it.)

The next step would be to do what Ben suggests and just
rewrite the terms in the ordered logistic, which would require
a bit more fancy indexing footwork, but could be implemented
pretty directly.

An integer binomial coefficient function would make things
cleaner.  All of this (n*(n+1))/2 stuff is just (n choose 2),
the sum of the numbers from 1 to n.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
HMC is rotation invariant, so correlations alone aren't
going to cause problems.  But it's not scale invariant.

Gibbs, on the other hand, is scale invariant, but not
rotation invariant.

Even basic HMC crushes Gibbs on unit-variance, highly-correlated
multivariate normals (assuming you don't cheat and have Gibbs
do a multivariate exact update!).

The varying step-size adaptation we do in Stan helps somewhat
with global scale issues, but can't deal with the local scale
issues exemplified with Neal's funnel distribution or
non-orthogonal scale exemplified by a multivariate normal with
high correlations and widely varying variances.

It's possible in some cases to transform the geometry of the
sampler and improve sampling.  The idea's to normalize the varying
scale introduced by parameters such as hierarchical deviation parameters
which have strong effects on lower-level parameters when the deviations
are tiny and highly constraining.

Ideally, you'd have both scale and rotation invariance, but doing that
requires something like Riemann Manifold HMC, which is very
computationally demanding (N^3 in the number of dimensions per
leapfrog step).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Actually, HMC is only rotation invariant with a scaled identity mass
matrix.  NUTS II breaks this, making its performance rotation
dependent because of the more general diagonal mass matrix.  However,
in general, NUTS II should always be better than NUTS I.

To illustrate, consider two independent variables one with small scale
and one with large scale.  With NUTS I, the mass is set based on the
smaller of the two scales and is unaffected by a rotation of the
parameter space.  NUTS II sets two different scales for the
independent variables, but when they're rotated it is forced to set
the scales based on the diagonal of the rotated scales which will be
somewhere between the smaller and larger scale and produce worse
performance than the unrotated case.

Cheers,
Marcus

means using the

option in the command line.

sizes (equivalently, diagonal mass matrix), which as Marcus
points out, is not rotation invariant.

> NUTS II breaks this, making its performance rotation

> in general, NUTS II should always be better than NUTS I.

Assuming it can adapt to the right per-variable scales during
warmup, of course.  So far, it's worked very well for us, but
there aren't any guarantees.

- Bob

On 11/16/12 5:48 PM, Ryan wrote:
> I have a model were I need to define many covariance matrices, but these covariance matrices are of varying sizes. For
> example, if I have n_i observations for each of N subjects, then I need to define something like cov_matrix[n_i] c_i for
> each N subjects. Is this possible to do in Stan so that I might be able to index them for each subject in the model
> code? From what I can tell in the documentation, and what I've found in this users group, it's not clear to me if this
> is possible except in the case where the n_i are the same for all N subjects.

I'm afraid it's not possible.  All the
variable declarations are rectangular.

It's not even easy to hack it the way you can
for the ordinal example from a few days ago
because the covariance matrix structure is
more complex (it could be done, but you'd need
to parameterize your own Cholesky factor then
do a lot of index fiddling to put things back
together again).

For a given fixed data set, it's possible to
explode out the model and index everything by
size.  But if there are lots of different values
for n_i[n], then that gets ugly.

We've been considering adding some ragged
data structures along the following lines:

   int<lower=0> N;          // number of subjects
   int<lower=1> n_obs[N];   // num observations for subject n in 1:N
   cov_matrix[n_obs] c;     // cov matrices for subject n in 1:N

The intent of the notation is that c[n] for n in 1:N
is an (n_obs[n] x n_obs[n]) covariance matrix.

This notation lets us do a single final layer of
raggedness and could apply anywhere there's a size.  So

    real y[n_obs];

could be used for the observations themselves.  y[n]
would be a size n_obs[n] array.

It's not something we're going to add right away
because of all the I/O and connections to R would
have to be upgraded.

- Bob

> Is there any way to save the state of the simulations, to inspect the chains and later on continue without the need to
> restart the simulations from the begining??

I'm afraid not.

There are two very different restart scenarios:

   (a) the sampler hasn't converged

   (b) the sampler has converged, but you need
       more effectife samples.

In the case of (a), we usually don't want to start
where we left off, but rather let adaptation run
long.  And that requires starting where adaptation
left off, not at the last sample.

In case (b), it makes sense to restart from where you
left off using the adaptation from the first run.

You lose at most a factor of two from starting again
if you are doubling input sizes each time:

   1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K

vs. the number of samples if using restart:

   1K, 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K

So it hasn't been a big priority for us compared to things
like adding discrete samples and vectorizing auto dif
calculations and making multivariate models more efficient.

The information on the adaptation is available as
a comment in the command line version of Stan -- I don't
know if it's available through RStan (yet).  But there's
no good way yet to restart Stan in the post-adaptation phase
with adaptation values from a previous run.

- Bob

   and R, Stan uses 0 to encode false, and 1 to encode true.  The only
   conditional-like operator is \Verb|if_else()| and the only logical
   output operator is \Verb|step()|.

   hacked with various flavors of arithmetic.  To test if a variable
   \code{x} is greater than or equal to \code{y}, use \code{step(x - y)}.
   To test if \code{x} equals \code{y}, use \code{step(x-y) * step(y-x)};
   to test for zero, use \code{step(x) * step(-x)}.

That will overflow for large y.  But we can compute stably on the
log scale, which is what we need anyway:

   log poisson_cdf(y|lamba)

   = -lambda + log SUM_{n=0}^y pow(lambda,n) / gamma(n+1)

   = -lambda + LOG_SUM_EXP_{n=0}^y log[pow(lambda,n) / gamma(n+1)]

   = -lambda + LOG_SUM_EXP_{n=0}^y [n * log(lambda) - lgamma(n+1)]

This should work for very modestly sized y.  But with y values
of any size, the loops will be slow and consume a lot of space on
the auto-dif stack.

I sure hope there's an efficient incomplete gamma on the
log scale the way there's an efficient log gamma function.
Michael's been looking into not only the CDFs, but their
gradients.

Hi All,

Following a JAGS example on John Kruschke's blog, I am trying to do a model comparison to obtain p(M1|D) / p(M2|D), for a simple model and a more sophisticated model.

In his examples, he often samples from dcat:

modelIndex ~ dcat( modelProbability[] )

where I take modelProbability to be a vector of {0.5,0.5} and so modelIndex "emits" 1 or 2.  Then, I can use an expression like:

a[g] <- mu[g] * kappa[g] * (modelIndex - 1) + mu0 * kappa0 * (2-modelIndex)

and a similar expression for b[g].

My questions:
1) when I try my Stan incarnation (please see attached files for code and sample data), modelIndex which I model in a similar way is zero!  Hence, the trick won't work.  Is there a proper Stan idiom?

2) If I were able to pull this off, how would I "aggregate" the values of modelIndex so that I can take the ratio of 1's and 2's to get the ratio that I seek?  It seems that parameters may only be real, and I haven't figured out how to cast the integer modelIndex into a real-declared variable due to what appears to be visibility/scope.

Thanks,
Eric

Stan does not yet support sampling of discrete parameters that have parents with other parameters. See sections 1.3 and 9.1 of the manual, for some discussion.

So the Metropolis-Hastings-Green trick I think you are attempting just won't work yet in Stan. Likewise, it's not possible to do imputation or measurement error on discrete data types.

messages.subject: operation result types: arrays, vecs, matrices
messages.subject_clean: operation result types: arrays, vecs, matrices
messages.body_plain:
On 11/24/12 10:41 AM, HookahBoy wrote:

> I am still a bit fuzzy about arrays, vectors, and matrices in Stan. In particular, some of the issues relating to what
> final form results from an operation on any two of these basic types and also how Stan is structured to prefer one form
> over the other in terms of efficiency.

As Ben said, don't worry about the efficiency.  Whatever
you do, it's negligible compared to the gradient calculations.
Even if you define things by component in a loop, the loops are
compiled.

Here's how to infer the type of an expression:

   literal  1    integer

   literal  1.0  real

   variable x    given by declaration (no hiding, so only one)

   x[i1,...,iN]  knock N indices off of type of x
                 (knocking one index off of matrix gives row vector,
                  one index off of vector or row_vector gives real)

   f(e1,...,eN)  figure out types of subexpressions
                 e1,...,eN, look up f in the appendix
                 and read off the result type
                (int types may be promoted to real if necessary)

In looking up functions, binary operators like * are
defined as operator*() in the documentation and index.

Matrices declared as:

   matrix[M,N] x[I,J];

are indexed as x[i,j,m,n] -- the array indices come first.

Also, all of the matrix operations are defined to return
the lowest inferrable type;  for example,

   row_vector * vector

produces a real, not a matrix.

I'll write a section to this effect in the manual so I
can just point to it in the future.

- Bob

Stan/RStan 1.0.4 is pretty much ready to go
other than some test issues.  We may not have
time to do the release for a week or two given
our various travel schedules.

Here's what's in it so far (though I may have missed
something and the jury's still out on changing categorical()
support from 0:(N-1) to 1:N and on removing non-symmetric
eigenvalues() functions):

v1.0.4
======================================================================
-- Libraries Updated
    * Eigen version 3.1.1 replaced with version 3.1.2
    * Boost version 1.51.0 replaced with version 1.52.0
-- Bug Fixes
    * fixed bug introduced in 1.0.3 that hid line and column number
      bug reporting
    * added checks that data dimensions match as well as sizes
    * removed non-symmetric versions of eigenvalues() and eigenvectors()
-- Improvements
    * generating double-based log-prob function (in addition to
      stan::agrad::var-based)
    * testing identifiers are not reserved words in C++/Stan
    * trapping/reporting locations of errors in data and init reads
    * templated out matrix libs to reduce code duplication
    * generalized multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose() to non-square
      matrices
    * vectorized auto-dif for tcrossprod() and crossprod()
-- New Functions
    * special functions: log_inv_logit(), log1m_inv_logit()
    * matrix special functions: cumulative_sum()
    * probability functions: poisson_log_log() for log-rate
      parameterized Poisson
    * matrix functions: block(), diag_pre_multiply(), diag_post_multiply()

- Bob

Dear Stan users:

We have developed Stan using partial support from several different research grants involving statistical modeling, computation, and applications. Continued development of Stan will be facilitated by continued outside funding.

Here's a way that some of you can help:  If you are putting together a grant proposal for a project in which you would be, or would like to be, using Stan, you could write us into your grant.  Support for a postdoc or programmer can help us with general Stan goals (ranging from implementation and optimization of specific model classes, to improvements in areas such as discrete sampling, to new developments in the sampling algorithms and new data structures) and, perhaps more to the point for your grant, we can devote effort to making your particular problem work in Stan.

What we get are the funds to move rapidly forward on our research and development work, thus making Stan both more awesome and more generally useful, both to applied users and to researchers.  What you get is an investment in practical and efficient computation for your problem, along with a say in the direction of where Stan goes next..

If this interests you, please contact us directly and we can talk about details!

Yours,
Andrew, Bob, and the rest of the Stan development team

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Save the state of the simulations to inspect the chains and continue the simulations?
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for resurrecting an old thread.  This question is probably due to my fuzzy understanding of HMC + NUTS.  My understanding is that the warmup stage calculates the step_size and the step_size multipliers. Would it make sense to allow for initial values of the step_size and the individual parameter step size multipliers? Or to allow for specifying fixed step size multipliers,  something equivalent to the option --equal_step_sizes, but using an arbitrary mass matrix?  "--epsilon=e --step_size_multipliers=1,1.5,2,0.5"?

- Jeff

On Sunday, November 18, 2012 5:06:52 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
>
> On 11/18/12 4:47 PM, John Aponte wrote:
> > Is there any way to save the state of the simulations, to inspect the chains and later on continue without the need to
> > restart the simulations from the begining??
>
> I'm afraid not.
>
> There are two very different restart scenarios:
>
>    (a) the sampler hasn't converged
>
>    (b) the sampler has converged, but you need
>        more effectife samples.
>
> In the case of (a), we usually don't want to start
> where we left off, but rather let adaptation run
> long.  And that requires starting where adaptation
> left off, not at the last sample.
>
> In case (b), it makes sense to restart from where you
> left off using the adaptation from the first run.
>
> You lose at most a factor of two from starting again
> if you are doubling input sizes each time:
>
>    1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K
>
> vs. the number of samples if using restart:
>
>    1K, 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K
>
> So it hasn't been a big priority for us compared to things
> like adding discrete samples and vectorizing auto dif
> calculations and making multivariate models more efficient.
>
> The information on the adaptation is available as
> a comment in the command line version of Stan -- I don't
> know if it's available through RStan (yet).  But there's
> no good way yet to restart Stan in the post-adaptation phase
> with adaptation values from a previous run.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>

On 11/27/12 10:29 PM, Jeffrey Arnold wrote:
> Sorry for resurrecting an old thread.  This question is probably due to my fuzzy understanding of HMC + NUTS.  My
> understanding is that the warmup stage calculates the step_size and the step_size multipliers. Would it make sense to
> allow for initial values of the step_size and the individual parameter step size multipliers? Or to allow for specifying
> fixed step size multipliers,  something equivalent to the option --equal_step_sizes, but using an arbitrary mass
> matrix?  "--epsilon=e --step_size_multipliers=1,1.5,2,0.5"?

Absolutely.  It's on our to-do list.

I'm not sure a command-line list is the way to go.  Some models
have thousands of params and most OS-es put some kind of limit
on the size of the command-line text.  So we probably want a file
format.

Technically, the current NUTS-II implementation in Stan uses
varying step sizes per dimension, not a mass matrix.  Radford
Neal discusses this in his MCMC handbook paper on HMC in section
5.4.2.4 <http://5.4.2.4>:

http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookChapter5.pdf

A Columbia Stats Dept. grad student, Yuanjun Guo, is working on
generalizing the adaptation from varying step sizes to full
mass matrices.  At that point, the command-line's not going
to be very workable for input.  And then we'll probably want
to look at some low-rank approximations.

We're also looking into doing Riemann Manifold HMC with
a diagonal mass matrix, which would be fairly easy to
compute (it needs third-order derivatives, but we could
add that capability), and would completely get around
trying to estimate a fixed mass matrix, which we know
doesn't work well for distributions whose posterior
covariance is position dependent.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Low tree depth and bad mixing probably
means the step size is too large in that region
and there's too much rejection going on.

Is this why you were asking about input of varying
step sizes?  What I'd suggest doing is using smaller
step size(s), but as you pointed out in the last message,
we don't have a way to let you do that!

One thing you might try to get out of it is turn
on the epsilon_pm parameter and let the step size
get significantly smaller.  It'll slow everything
else down, but it may allow you to mix in bad regions.

We've also been considering automatically lowering
the step size every 10th iteration or so.

Another thing that can help is reparameterizing so
the posterior space is better behaved.  What we've
been calling the "Matt trick", because he introduced
it.  There's an example in the manual for the new release.
But the basic idea in the simplest case
is that rather than doing this:

   for (n in 1:N)
     alpha[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);

   ... use alpha[n] ...

do this:

   for (n in 1:N)
     alpha_raw[n] ~ normal(0,1);

   ... use (mu + sigma * alpha_raw[n]) ...

I really wish we could do this kind of transform automatically!

- Bob

On Tuesday, November 27, 2012 11:00:52 PM UTC-5, Jeffrey Arnold wrote:
> Sorry that I couldn't make it simpler, I don't expect you to work through the model; I was just wondering if you have any ideas of what sort of problems this chain behavior might indicate.

Bob stated the Matt trick in general, and there are a few examples of it on the list or in the manual. If you search for "random walk" on stan-users, there are a couple of things that are more pertinent to your situation. In particular, I think you would want to make a theta_innovation parameter with a standard normal prior and then make theta a transformed parameter that is theta[i] <- theta[i-1] + sigma * theta_innovation[i].

Also, the constraint that the loadings matrix is unit lower-triangular is convenient, but it does make all the free parameters sensitive to the first n_factors outcome variables. If those outcomes are not that germane, or have a small amount of common variance, or have very different variances, then you could get computational problems. So, you might try reordering the outcomes to put the theoretically best ones first.

Ben

> generalizing the adaptation from varying step sizes to full
> mass matrices.  At that point, the command-line's not going
> to be very workable for input.  And then we'll probably want
> to look at some low-rank approximations.
>
> We're also looking into doing Riemann Manifold HMC with
> a diagonal mass matrix, which would be fairly easy to
> compute (it needs third-order derivatives, but we could
> add that capability), and would completely get around
> trying to estimate a fixed mass matrix, which we know
> doesn't work well for distributions whose posterior
> covariance is position dependent.
>
> - Bob
>
> >

> >
> >
> >
> >
> >     On 11/18/12 4:47 PM, John Aponte wrote:

> >     need to
> >      > restart the simulations from the begining??
> >
> >     I'm afraid not.
> >
> >     There are two very different restart scenarios:
> >
> >         (a) the sampler hasn't converged
> >
> >         (b) the sampler has converged, but you need
> >             more effectife samples.
> >
> >     In the case of (a), we usually don't want to start
> >     where we left off, but rather let adaptation run
> >     long.  And that requires starting where adaptation
> >     left off, not at the last sample.
> >
> >     In case (b), it makes sense to restart from where you
> >     left off using the adaptation from the first run.
> >
> >     You lose at most a factor of two from starting again
> >     if you are doubling input sizes each time:
> >
> >         1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K
> >
> >     vs. the number of samples if using restart:
> >
> >         1K, 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K
> >
> >     So it hasn't been a big priority for us compared to things
> >     like adding discrete samples and vectorizing auto dif
> >     calculations and making multivariate models more efficient.
> >
> >     The information on the adaptation is available as
> >     a comment in the command line version of Stan -- I don't

Model name=firstmodel_model
Input file=/Users/carp/temp2/firstmodel.stan

          ^-- here

Parser expecting: <list><expression>","

The issue is that Stan doesn't support partial array/vector/matrix
notation, so you can't do what you're trying to do.

If you have an M x N matrix x, then x[m] is a N-row-vector.
and for an M x N array y, y[m] is an N-array.

 In short yes, high correlations can exacerbate the problem of differing scales. I think Marcus gave the best explanation at

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/2YMo3SUzHTg/4xfu1IKVT78J

but be sure to unhide the quoted text to see the rest of it.

If theta were a parameter and

theta[i] ~ normal(theta[i-1], sigma)

then the joint distribution of theta[i], theta[i-1], and sigma is very correlated. Conversely, if theta_innovation is parameter with iid standard normal priors, then they've got the same scale and no dependence, at least a priori. Then, theta is a transformed parameter such that

theta[i] <- theta[i-1] * sigma * theta_innovation[i]

which may affect the likelihood of the data but doesn't get a prior.

I think there is also a sense in which Stan is optimized for sampling from independent standard normals with the way the momentum and leapfrogging works, so whatever you can do to make the posterior distribution be closer to N(0,I) is good.

Ben

It's not tied to normality or correlation per se.

If the eigenvalues are all the same, Stan will work equally
well no matter what the rotation is.

Basic HMC is rotation invariant, but it's not scale invariant.

Stan's varying step sizes rescale each dimension
which destroys the rotation invariance.

But the really big issue is the position-dependent geometry of
the posterior.  Specifically, in a hierarchical model,
when the hierarchical variance is low, the scale of
the lower level parameters will be low, and when it's
high, the scale will be high.  This is clearly illustrated
with Radford Neal's funnel density.  I did a plot and provide
the reparameterization.  I put the draft of the relevant section
up on out code page:

http://code.google.com/p/stan/downloads/detail?name=stan-reference-1.0.4-draft-reparam.pdf

As an added bonus, you get a section from Ben on multivariate
reparameterizations.

There's more to come in this section.  The normal isn't the
only thing that can get reparameterized this way.

And, as Ben points out, we'd ideally like to standardize
the posterior, but we don't know what that is, or we
wouldn't be doing MCMC in the first place!

- Bob

...

--epsilon=<double> pins the basic step size to that value.

--equal_step_sizes turns off varying step size adaptation.

Setting both of these will use --epsilon for the step size
in each dimension with no adaptation whatsoever.

--L=<int> sets the number of leapfrog steps (and turns off NUTS)

If you don't use --L, then NUTS determines the number of steps.

>
> This is somewhat related, but does parameter expansion have any effect in Stan?

I'll quote from Matt, who's much more articulate on
these matters:

 From Matt Hoffman, 14 Aug 2012
=========================================
All I did was replace the hierarchical prior

σ ~ U(0, 1000)
μ ~ N(0, 1000)
θ_j ~ N(μ, σ)

with the equivalent non-hierarchical prior

σ ~ U(0, 1000)
μ ~ N(0, 1000)
\tilde θ_j ~ N(0, 1)
θ_j = \tilde θ_j * σ + μ.

Basically, it's just a change of variables that makes the nasty
heavy-tailed hierarchical prior into a simple product prior on a
different measure space. In graphical model terms, this reads as
taking apart the hierarchy and making all of the nodes point directly
at the data.

Empirically, the model as originally written fails to get into the
left tail of σ (and rejects a lot when it gets close), whereas the
reparameterized model has no such problems. Mixing also seems faster,
which isn't too surprising, given that the reparameterized model has a
much smaller range of log-probabilities (std. dev. of about 2.6)
compared with the original model (std. dev. of about 6.5).
=========================================

It's like the funnel only a more realistic example and Matt
throws in an explanation of why it works.

 > More generally, a list of which
> heuristics / tricks from gibbs sampling carry over to HMC would be very useful.

We're still working a lot of that out ourselves!

What will help most for Stan is any transformation that
makes the posterior more like N(0,I).

Either scaling or rotation on their own should be OK,
but together they can be problematic.

In general, it helps to apply transforms if they

  -- eliminate varying scales in different parts of the posterior
     that would ideally be suited to different step sizes
  -- anything that gets rid of correlation related to the above

The funnel transform is an example of both.  Also,

  -- anything that makes the scale more uniform
     at varying points in the space

For the artificial funnel example, there's strong correlation
driving position-dependent scaling, which is easy to convert
to unit normal.

  -- anything that makes thin tails or thick tails more normal

The above example from Matt is an example of thinning the tails,
and the triangle distribution (in the current v.1.0.3 manual)
by transforming through constraints -- that's an implicit logit
transform that changes the tail behavior.

Anyone else have anything else for the list?  I can include
it in the reparameterization section of the manual.

- Bob

I'm glad it's working for you.  But keep in mind it's
not the number of iterations that matter, it's how many
effective samples they produce.

Stan 1.0.3 can crash R due to index out of bounds
errors in the C++.  That should be fixed for 1.0.4
with warning messages.

Stan can also crash R by exhausting memory, but that's
unlikely to happen right out of the gate with the
fairly small data set you have.

So you might want to try ramping the model complexity
back up a bit.  I think most of the uncaught errors
were during data ingestion.

The time per iteration is dominated by the gradient calcs,
and we're making those faster all the time.
Daniel's added a whole bunch of vectorized probabilty
function code for 1.0.4 and over the next few months,
we'll have them all properly vectorized, including
multivariates.  And we're going to tackle the matrix
ops, too -- right now the gradients are being done
very inefficiently by auto-dif and in many cases, we
have analytic solutions we can plug in to make things
much faster.

I have a hierarchical model in JAGS.  Appears to work fine, but takes forever on my current machine (latest core, i7, 16GB RAM, etc.)  So, I want to try things in stan.

Two questions:
1) Will it run faster/better from the command line than from within R with the rstan package?

2) Can someone help me with the format of the model file.  I'm having trouble understanding how to convert this jags code to stan code.  This is a hierarchical model with factors for both "group" and "program".  Looking at counts of students based on their group membership. (Pre-defined cluster) and the program they might enroll

Thanks!

Model below
================================

model{

    for(i in 1:N){
        eta[i] <-  ranef_group[group[i]] + ranef_prog[program[i]]+ b_var_1 * var_1[i] + b_var_2 * var_2[i]  + b_var_3 * var_3[i]
        log(lambda[i]) <- eta[i]
        count[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])

    b_var_3 ~ dnorm(0, tau_var_3)

    tau_var_1 <- pow(sigma_var_1, -2)
    tau_var_2 <- pow(sigma_var_2, -2)
    tau_var_3 <- pow(sigma_var_3, -2)
    tau_group <- pow(sigma_group, -2)
    tau_prog <- pow(sigma_prog, -2)

    sigma_var_1 ~ dunif(0,100)
    sigma_var_2 ~ dunif(0,100)
    sigma_var_3 ~ dunif(0,100)
    sigma_group ~ dunif(0,100)
    sigma_prog ~ dunif(0,100)

    for (i in 1:n_group){
        ranef_group[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau_group)
    }

    for (i in 1:n_prog){
        ranef_prog[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau_prog)
    }
}

The error in here: In Stan, you need to indicate the support of variables that have bounded support, such as non-negative variances. So, you need

real<lower=0> sigma_var_1;

The error you got was due to Stan proposing a value of sigma_var_1 that was negative, in which case the uniform(0,100) becomes undefined.

I would suggest reading Appendix C of the Stan manual and this FAQ

Ben

On 11/30/12 12:20 PM, Noah wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I have a hierarchical model in JAGS.  Appears to work fine, but takes forever on my current machine (latest core, i7,
> 16GB RAM, etc.)  So, I want to try things in stan.
>
> Two questions:
> 1) Will it run faster/better from the command line than from within R with the rstan package?

It runs the same compiled code.  There's a bit of
overhead from using R, but that's only in getting
data in and out.  It can take more size to store the
data in R, too.

> 2) Can someone help me with the format of the model file.  I'm having trouble understanding how to convert this jags
> code to stan code.  This is a hierarchical model with factors for both "group" and "program".  Looking at counts of
> students based on their group membership. (Pre-defined cluster) and the program they might enroll
>
> Thanks!
>
> Model below
> ================================

You need to declare data and parameters.  Look in
the manual to see how to do that, and make sure
you get the constraints on the deviation parameters sigma.

> model{
>
>      for(i in 1:N){
>          eta[i] <-  ranef_group[group[i]] + ranef_prog[program[i]]+ b_var_1 * var_1[i] + b_var_2 * var_2[i]  + b_var_3 *
> var_3[i]
>          log(lambda[i]) <- eta[i]

No reason to make this separate, you just do

    lambda[i] <- exp(eta[i]);

>          count[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])

You can just do this in Stan:

   count[i] ~ poisson(exp(lambda[i]));

>      }
>
>      b_var_1    ~ dnorm(0, tau_var_1)

     b_var_1 ~ normal(0,sigma_var_1);

>      b_var_2 ~ dnorm(0, tau_var_2)
>      b_var_3 ~ dnorm(0, tau_var_3)
>
>      tau_var_1 <- pow(sigma_var_1, -2)
>      tau_var_2 <- pow(sigma_var_2, -2)
>      tau_var_3 <- pow(sigma_var_3, -2)
>      tau_group <- pow(sigma_group, -2)
>      tau_prog <- pow(sigma_prog, -2)
>
>      sigma_var_1 ~ dunif(0,100)
>      sigma_var_2 ~ dunif(0,100)
>      sigma_var_3 ~ dunif(0,100)
>      sigma_group ~ dunif(0,100)
>      sigma_prog ~ dunif(0,100)
>
>
>      for (i in 1:n_group){
>          ranef_group[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau_group)
>      }
>
>      for (i in 1:n_prog){
>          ranef_prog[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau_prog)
>      }
> }

Also, things get executed in order, so that if
you did want to transform a variable for using it with <-
then you need to do it BEFORE using it.

- Bob

On Thursday, November 29, 2012 12:48:01 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> On 11/28/12 11:44 PM, Jeffrey Arnold wrote:
> > Thanks Ben and Bob. I have a somewhat better intuition now.  That part of the reference manual looks really good.
> >
> > This is somewhat related, but does parameter expansion have any effect in Stan?
>
> I'll quote from Matt, who's much more articulate on
> these matters:
>
>  From Matt Hoffman, 14 Aug 2012
> =========================================
> All I did was replace the hierarchical prior
>
> σ ~ U(0, 1000)
> μ ~ N(0, 1000)
> θ_j ~ N(μ, σ)
>
> with the equivalent non-hierarchical prior
>
> σ ~ U(0, 1000)
> μ ~ N(0, 1000)
> \tilde θ_j ~ N(0, 1)
> θ_j = \tilde θ_j * σ + μ.
>
> Basically, it's just a change of variables that makes the nasty
> heavy-tailed hierarchical prior into a simple product prior on a
> different measure space. In graphical model terms, this reads as
> taking apart the hierarchy and making all of the nodes point directly
> at the data.
>
> Empirically, the model as originally written fails to get into the
> left tail of σ (and rejects a lot when it gets close), whereas the
> reparameterized model has no such problems. Mixing also seems faster,
> which isn't too surprising, given that the reparameterized model has a
> much smaller range of log-probabilities (std. dev. of about 2.6)
> compared with the original model (std. dev. of about 6.5).
> =========================================
>
> It's like the funnel only a more realistic example and Matt
> throws in an explanation of why it works.
>
>  > More generally, a list of which
> > heuristics / tricks from gibbs sampling carry over to HMC would be very useful.
>
> We're still working a lot of that out ourselves!
>
> What will help most for Stan is any transformation that
> makes the posterior more like N(0,I).
>
> Either scaling or rotation on their own should be OK,
> but together they can be problematic.
>
> In general, it helps to apply transforms if they
>
>   -- eliminate varying scales in different parts of the posterior
>      that would ideally be suited to different step sizes
>   -- anything that gets rid of correlation related to the above
>
> The funnel transform is an example of both.  Also,
>
>   -- anything that makes the scale more uniform
>      at varying points in the space
>
> For the artificial funnel example, there's strong correlation
> driving position-dependent scaling, which is easy to convert
> to unit normal.
>
>   -- anything that makes thin tails or thick tails more normal
>
> The above example from Matt is an example of thinning the tails,
> and the triangle distribution (in the current v.1.0.3 manual)
> by transforming through constraints -- that's an implicit logit
> transform that changes the tail behavior.
>
> Anyone else have anything else for the list?  I can include
> it in the reparameterization section of the manual.
>
> - Bob
>
